title: Cervical spine examination

guidelineVersions: BJGP 2018 review of cervical radiculopathy and myelopathy

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee assessing a 58-year-old patient with six months of neck stiffness and intermittent tingling in the right hand. There has been no recent trauma.
brief.task: Conduct a focused cervical spine and neurological examination and report whether the findings suggest radiculopathy or cervical myelopathy. Request findings from the examiner for steps that cannot be simulated.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: This patient has a possible spinal cord problem hidden beneath ordinary neck discomfort. Look for gait and upper motor-neurone signs as well as radicular findings.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Stopping after neck range of movement and a sensory check, missing hand clumsiness and lower limb signs.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: “Before testing movement, I want to ask about hand dexterity, walking and bladder symptoms; then examine safely.”

flow: 0–1 min: consent, pain, trauma/instability screen and red flags
1–3 min: inspect head posture, upper limbs, scars and cautious active neck movements
3–5 min: upper limb power, sensation, reflexes and hand dexterity
5–7 min: gait, lower limb tone/reflexes and plantar responses; interpret Hoffmann sign cautiously
7–9 min: summarise possible myelopathy, urgent specialist review/imaging and safety advice

grid.label: Safe introduction and red flags
grid.fail: Forcefully moves painful neck without checking safety
grid.borderline: Consent but no trauma or cord history
grid.pass: Consent, pain assessment, screens recent trauma, weakness, gait or bladder disturbance
grid.high: Prioritises cord-warning symptoms before provocative manoeuvres

grid.label: Inspection and range of movement
grid.pass: Inspects posture/scars and assesses comfortable active range only
grid.high: Stops provocative movement if it causes neurological worsening

grid.label: Upper limb motor examination
grid.pass: Tests representative C5–T1 myotomes and compares sides
grid.high: Also examines fine finger movement and functional hand dexterity

grid.label: Upper limb sensation
grid.pass: Assesses light touch in C5–T1 pattern bilaterally and distinguishes dermatomal from patchy loss
grid.high: Correlates sensory pattern with motor and reflex changes rather than naming a root prematurely

grid.label: Deep tendon reflexes
grid.pass: Checks biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes bilaterally
grid.high: Recognises brisk reflexes may imply cord involvement, while depressed root reflexes may indicate radiculopathy

grid.label: Myelopathy screening
grid.borderline: Asks about falls but does not examine gait
grid.pass: Assesses gait, lower limb reflexes and plantar responses as indicated; interprets upper motor-neurone features
grid.high: Uses Hoffmann sign as a supporting, not definitive, sign and integrates hand dexterity and gait

grid.label: Synthesis
grid.fail: Calls this simple strain despite objective neurological deficits
grid.pass: Recognises possible degenerative cervical myelopathy with radicular symptoms
grid.high: Separates clinical suspicion from confirmation and identifies urgent imaging/specialist pathway

grid.label: Escalation and management
grid.fail: Offers routine physiotherapy only and defers referral
grid.pass: Arranges urgent senior/spinal assessment and MRI decision through local pathway
grid.high: Avoids cervical manipulation and communicates concern without declaring a confirmed diagnosis

grid.label: Communication and safety
grid.fail: Reassures despite progressive gait or bladder symptoms
grid.pass: Explains hand/gait deterioration and bladder/bowel warning symptoms and urgent help
grid.high: Checks patient understanding, documents objective findings and safe follow-up

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: You have neck stiffness. I’ll bend your head backwards to see how far it goes.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: That causes tingling in my hand.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Try harder; I need the full movement.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Squeeze my fingers. Good, your strength is fine.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The tingling is probably a pinched nerve. I do not need to compare sensation across the arms.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Reflexes are not important in a stiff neck, and gait is unrelated.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you ask about hand function or walking?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No. Stiffness and tingling at this age are just wear and tear. I will give you a physiotherapy leaflet.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The patient says they had a new bladder symptom yesterday.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That can wait until the next visit.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: There is no reason to involve one.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I’m the core surgical trainee. I would like to assess your neck, arms and walking to find out whether the nerves or spinal cord might be involved. Is that okay?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes. My neck is stiff, and my right hand tingles.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Before I move the neck, have you had a fall or injury? Any difficulty with buttons, dropping objects, balance or new bladder trouble?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No injury, and nothing I’ve noticed with my bladder, but I have dropped my keys and buttons are awkward. I am less steady on stairs.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I’ll look at head posture, muscles and scars, and ask you to turn your head only as far as comfortable. Tell me if you get pain or worsening tingling.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There is reduced active rotation, especially rightward, without pain shooting down the arm during the movement.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will compare shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and extension, wrist movements, finger extension and finger abduction, then ask you to open and close the hands rapidly.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Most power is 5 out of 5; right finger abduction is 4-plus out of 5, and rapid hand opening is slightly slow.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I’ll compare light touch across both arms and hands, including representative C5 to T1 areas. Is the sensation the same on each side?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There is intermittent altered light touch in the right index and middle fingers; the rest is preserved.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will check biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes bilaterally.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Biceps and brachioradialis are normal. Triceps reflexes are brisk on both sides.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Because of the hand difficulty, I must also observe gait and check lower limb reflexes and plantar responses.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Gait is broad-based, tandem gait is impaired, knee reflexes are brisk and plantar responses extensor bilaterally. Right Hoffmann is positive.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: These findings suggest possible cervical myelopathy, not isolated cervical radiculopathy. The altered finger sensation could reflect a root component, but the gait and brisk lower limb responses raise concern about the cord.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The patient asks: “Could I just have physiotherapy for my stiff neck?”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would not recommend cervical manipulation or routine physiotherapy as the only plan while we are concerned about cord compression. I would urgently discuss with the senior/spinal team and arrange appropriate cervical MRI assessment.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Does that mean permanent damage?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not necessarily. I cannot confirm the cause without specialist assessment and imaging, but the signs deserve prompt investigation because untreated cord problems may worsen.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Late cue: the patient remembers one episode of urinary urgency yesterday, without incontinence.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would clarify whether there is new retention, incontinence or progressive weakness and escalate the new symptom to the senior team now. Any sudden worsening of walking, weakness or bladder/bowel control needs urgent emergency assessment.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: I understand why we need to check this quickly.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I’m one of the core surgical trainees. May I examine your neck, arms and balance? With symptoms like hand clumsiness, I first want to rule out a spinal-cord warning sign before asking you to move your neck.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: That sounds sensible; I keep dropping keys.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Has there been trauma? Any progressive weakness, difficulty walking, changes in handwriting or fastening buttons, or bladder and bowel symptoms?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No injury. Buttons have become harder during the last six weeks and I am unsteady on stairs; nothing I’ve noticed with my bladder.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I’ll inspect posture, wasting and surgical scars. Please rotate gently within comfort; I will not force extension or use provocative manipulation.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Rotation is limited to the right. No scar or marked muscle wasting.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I’m testing power side to side from shoulder abduction down to intrinsic hand muscles and rapid finger movement, looking not just for an isolated root deficit but loss of fine motor control.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Right finger abduction 4+/5, the rest 5/5, with mildly slow rapid hand opening.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I’ll map sensation in the hands and forearms. Where exactly is the tingling?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Mainly the index and middle fingers of my right hand.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The corresponding light-touch change is intermittent. No widespread sensory deficit.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will compare biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes, then look for upper motor-neurone signs. The pattern of reflexes matters more than any single test.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Triceps brisk bilaterally, with other upper-limb reflexes normal.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Please walk a short distance with support nearby and, if safe, try heel-to-toe walking. I will check knee reflexes and plantar responses.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Broad-based walking, impaired tandem gait, brisk knees and bilateral extensor plantars. Right Hoffmann sign is positive.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The combined hand dexterity change, gait disturbance and long-tract signs strongly suggest cervical cord involvement. Hoffmann alone would not establish myelopathy, but here it reinforces the overall pattern. Coexisting root irritation could explain finger paraesthesia.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The patient asks if they can book a manipulation session later this week.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would advise against neck manipulation until spinal cord compression is assessed. I will discuss this urgently with the senior clinician/spinal service and request cervical MRI through the agreed pathway. I would record the exact motor, reflex and gait findings for the referral.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Am I going to lose the use of my hands?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I cannot predict that from this examination. The reason to investigate promptly is to reduce the risk of deterioration and clarify the treatment options, which may or may not involve surgery.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Final cue: “I’ve just remembered — I had unusual urinary urgency yesterday, but not incontinence.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That is relevant new information. I would ask about retention, loss of urinary control and saddle symptoms, document the chronology, and convey it immediately in my urgent senior referral; I would not leave this as a routine outpatient issue.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Until review, seek emergency care for worsening limb weakness, falls, or new bladder or bowel dysfunction. Can you tell me which changes would prompt you to seek help?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: A sudden change in walking, weakness, or bladder control.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Exactly. I will explain the plan and arrange the assessment now rather than simply sending you away with exercises.

failures.move: Forces neck motion despite neurological symptoms.
failures.consequence: May provoke pain or neurological deterioration in an unstable/cord-compromised patient.

failures.move: Ignores gait disturbance and upper motor-neurone signs.
failures.consequence: Misses possible cervical myelopathy and delays decompression assessment.

failures.move: Fails to escalate progressive neurological or new bladder symptoms.

recovery.when: If you attributed this to a simple nerve root problem
recovery.line: I should not attribute this to a simple nerve root problem without examining gait and long-tract signs; I will complete the cord examination now.

recovery.when: If the examination suggests possible myelopathy and you need to change your plan
recovery.line: I need to change my plan: the examination suggests possible myelopathy, so urgent senior and spinal assessment is appropriate.

knowledge.fact: Radiculopathy without red flags can usually be referred routinely to a spinal clinic, or for MRI if conservative measures fail; myelopathy features change the urgency.
Myelopathy presents with clumsy hands, reduced manual dexterity and an unsteady gait; neck pain may be absent. Ask about bladder and bowel function.
Hoffmann’s test has low reported sensitivity, so a negative result does not rule out myelopathy.
Examine both upper and lower limbs: myelopathy causes upper motor neurone signs, particularly in the legs (brisk reflexes, up-going plantars); clonus of more than 3 beats is highly suggestive.
Any positive myelopathy symptoms or signs warrant immediate referral, usually by phoning the on-call orthopaedic or spinal registrar.
In recent trauma, the assessment differs: spinal protection and formal injury risk stratification take priority over routine active movements.

recall.say: “Hand clumsiness and gait changes raise concern for myelopathy.”
do: upper-limb motor/sensory/reflex testing; gait and long-tract signs.

numbers.meaning: clonus of more than 3 beats is highly suggestive of myelopathy; no other threshold is required.

recall.trap: treating cord signs as benign radiculopathy.
recall.finish: urgent senior/spinal referral and appropriate MRI pathway; document and safety-net.

sources.name: McCartney S, Baskerville R, Blagg S, McCartney D. Cervical radiculopathy and cervical myelopathy: diagnosis and management in primary care.
sources.supports: myelopathy symptoms and signs, Hoffmann sensitivity, clonus, bladder/bowel enquiry, immediate referral for myelopathy, routine pathway for uncomplicated radiculopathy.

sources.name: NICE NG41, Spinal injury: assessment and initial management
sources.supports: separate traumatic/unstable spine protection; not a routine non-trauma range-of-motion guideline.

partner.opening: Conduct a focused cervical spine and neurological examination and report whether the findings suggest radiculopathy or cervical myelopathy.
partner.actorBrief: “My neck is stiff and my right hand tingles.” Fictional patient: 58 years old; neck stiffness for six months. Right index and middle finger paraesthesia intermittently; dropping keys for six weeks and difficulty fastening buttons. No trauma, fever or cancer history. Normal current bladder function. Only answer specific questions about dropping keys, buttons and gait when asked. If asked about bladder symptoms before the final cue, answer: “Nothing I’ve noticed.”

reveals.finding: upper limb power largely 5/5 with mild right finger-abduction weakness 4+/5.
Biceps reflexes normal; triceps brisk bilaterally.
Gait is wide-based and tandem gait is impaired.

reveals.trigger: On lower limb reflexes and plantars
reveals.finding: Knee reflexes brisk, plantar responses extensor bilaterally.
Hoffmann sign present on right (supportive only).

Examiner releases these findings only when requested. Give examination findings when each manoeuvre is performed or asked of the examiner. Candidate must not perform forced manipulation. Do not invent additional neurological findings.

curveballs.safeAnswer: I would clarify whether there is new retention, incontinence or progressive weakness and escalate the new symptom to the senior team now. Any sudden worsening of walking, weakness or bladder/bowel control needs urgent emergency assessment.
